segments: 344. Chronography of Barhebraeus.

And in this year, which is 1487 [of the Greeks],
567 of the Arabs [= 1171/2 AD],
Nūr al-Dīn sent to Saladin
that he should abolish the proclamation [of the Friday prayer] for al-ʿĀḍid, the Caliph of Egypt,
and proclaim the Caliph of Baghdad.
And since Saladin was afraid of the Egyptians, lest they should make a commotion against him,
he delayed the matter.
Then Nūr al-Dīn compelled him to do so.
And since he was not able to transgress his command,
he took counsel with the nobles as to how this should be done.
And when some of them were saying that it was possible,
and some of them that it was not possible,
there was present there a Persian man who was called the Amir the Teacher [al-Amir al-Alim].
He said to them,
"I will make the proclamation first,
and you be freed from anxiety."
And when the day of Friday arrived,
that man approached and went up onto the pulpit (bema),
and instead of al-ʿĀḍid the son of ʿAlī,
he named al-Mustaḍīʾ the son of al-ʿAbbās.
And no one was able to murmur.
And so on the next Friday, when the rest of the preachers were ordered,
they too made the proclamation in all the mosques.
And thus the Caliphate of the Egyptians came to an end.
Now as for the Caliph al-ʿĀḍid,
because he was sick in those days,
his people did not inform him of what had happened,
lest they distress him and he die.
And he died without being aware of it.
Then Saladin imprisoned his sons and his household,
and separated the males among them from the females,
so that their lineage might be cut off.
And so it was.
And he set free his male and female slaves.
And there was rejoicing among the members of the sect of the Sunnis {OCR?} among the Arabs,
because the kingdom of the sect of the advocates of liberty and autonomy had been brought to an end.
And they say
that their lineage was not from ʿAlī and Fāṭimah, as they used to claim,
but from a certain Jew or a Magian.
And poets also composed many verses [stating],
"The Pharaonic kingdom has indeed ended,
and the Josephite [Ayyubid] has begun."
Fourteen [caliphs] arose in the West:
three of them in Africa [Ifrīqiyā]:
al-Mahdī,
al-Qāʾim,
al-Manṣūr;
and eleven in Egypt:
al-Muʿizz,
al-ʿAzīz,
al-Ḥākim,
al-Ẓāhir,
al-Mustanṣir,
al-Mustaʿlī,
al-Āmir,
al-Ḥāfiẓ,
al-Ẓāfir,
al-Fāʾiz,
al-ʿĀḍid.
